progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From bio-m5-b06a: prokaryotes have no nucleus, their DNA sits in the cytoplasm (the nucleoid); eukaryotic cells have a nucleus; cells contain ribosomes. From B2c (route bio-m5-b02b), background only: a bacterium is a single cell that copies itself by splitting in two. From Year 11 Module 1: cells, cell walls, the cytoplasm, proteins and nucleic acids (DNA and RNA). Not assumed: infectious against non-infectious, pathogen, host, the three groups, fungi and protozoa as pathogens, helminths, viruses as non-cellular, viroids, prions, why drugs are group-specific.
progression.startsWith: Separate infectious from non-infectious disease and sort pathogens by structure. The video opens: In 1928, Alexander Fleming noticed a mould growing on one of his culture dishes.
progression.stopsAfter: defining an infectious disease as one caused by a pathogen (most can pass between hosts), with tuberculosis against type 2 diabetes, and noting that most microbes are not pathogens; sorting pathogens by whether they are made of cells, and then whether they are many-celled animals, into microorganisms (bacteria, fungi, protozoa), macroorganisms (helminths, ectoparasites) and non-cellular pathogens (viruses, viroids, prions); describing each type's key structure with a named disease and its true relative size; distinguishing viroids (RNA only, known in plants) from prions (protein only, misfolding normal proteins, known in animals); showing the same groups in plants; explaining that a treatment must target something the pathogen has and the host lacks, so antibiotics act on bacteria but not on viruses or prions; classifying three unseen agents with justification and explaining an antibiotic's action on bovine TB but not BSE.
progression.nextLesson: how Pasteur and Koch showed that microbes come from other microbes and that a specific microbe causes a specific disease (route entry bio-m7-b02).

teaching.task: What makes a disease infectious, and why does knowing which kind of pathogen causes it decide how it can be treated?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: why a disease spreads (the pathogen passes between hosts, 2); why viruses are not microorganisms (not cells, 3); why bacteria differ from fungi and protozoa (nucleus, 4); why a virus needs a host cell (no ribosomes or cytoplasm, 6); how a prion spreads with no genes (converting normal copies, 7); why drugs are group-specific (a target the host lacks, 9). Visible case: the clear ring around the mould; the jump between host circles; the zoom ladder with true-scale pairs; the misfolding row; the tree filling with plant cases and treatment chips. Thinking opportunities: two unseen items. Reading load: at most about three bright text items; the full tree in scene 8 is the densest frame, so its leaf labels are small and grey and only the newest plant tag is bright.
teaching.conversationalApproach: Fleming's mould killed the bacteria around it and led to penicillin, yet penicillin does nothing against many infections, so the question is what makes a disease infectious and why the kind of pathogen decides how it can be treated; an infectious disease is caused by a pathogen living in or on a host and harming it, and most can pass between hosts. The SorterTree then sorts pathogens with one question at a time: is it made of cells (microorganisms against macroorganisms and non-cellular agents), does the cell have a nucleus (bacteria as prokaryotes, against fungi and protozoa), which macroorganisms are parasitic animals (helminths inside, ectoparasites outside), and for non-cellular pathogens whether it is genes in a protein coat (a virus), RNA only (a viroid) or protein only (a prion), with plants as hosts too; a drug has to hit something the pathogen has and the host does not, so the group decides treatment. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: In 1928, Alexander Fleming noticed a mould growing on one of his culture dishes. Around it, the bacteria had died, leaving a clear ring. That mould led to penicillin. But penicillin does nothing for the flu, for tinea, for malaria or for a tapeworm. So what makes a disease infectious, and why does the kind of pathogen decide how we can fight it?
teaching.understandingCheck: 11a is a classify-and-justify item: three agents described only by their structure (a single cell with its own nucleus and no wall inside a bird's red blood cells; a small circle of RNA with no protein coat from deformed potato tubers; a flat segmented worm two metres long from a dog's intestine). It tests the sorting questions on new descriptions with no plates (a plate would give the answer away). 11c is an explain item: bovine tuberculosis (a rod-shaped bacterium) against BSE (a prion); explain why an antibiotic could act on one pathogen but not the other. It tests the treatment link. Each ends "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; the whole card stays on screen during the countdown and after it. Each feedback is brief (about 20 to 25 s): the answer, the key reason, givens underlined in the question strip as they are used, one crossed-out classic mistake. No givens card.
teaching.curriculumScope: B7-IQ1-01: "describe a variety of infectious diseases caused by pathogens, including microorganisms, macroorganisms and non-cellular pathogens, and collect primary and secondary-sourced data and information relating to disease transmission, including: (ACSBL097, ACSBL098, ACSBL116, ACSBL117)", with its listed example "classifying different pathogens that cause disease in plants and animals (ACSBL117)". This video covers the "describe a variety of infectious diseases caused by pathogens, including microorganisms, macroorganisms and non-cellular pathogens" stem and the classifying example. The data-collection stem and the other three examples (epidemic transmission, microbial testing of water or food, modes of transmission) stay open for b03, p01 and p02. Verbs: "describe" (scenes 2 to 8: named diseases with their pathogens) and "classify", which NESA examines as distinguish or identify with justification (scenes 3 to 8 and attempt 1); the treatment link (scene 9 and attempt 2) is an "explain".

design.visualSystem: One pathogen sorter: a branching tree drawn in code on the dark board. Root node "pathogen"; first fork "made of cells?" into three branches, "microorganisms", "macroorganisms" and "non-cellular"; leaves "bacteria", "fungi", "protozoa" | "helminths", "ectoparasites" | "viruses", "viroids", "prions". Each leaf is headed by its painted plate thumbnail. The tree builds branch by branch in scenes 3 to 7, the plant examples join beside the leaves in scene 8, and in scene 9 each leaf gains a small treatment chip. A size ruler (a coded horizontal scale bar whose label changes: metres, millimetres, thousandths of a millimetre, ten-thousandths of a millimetre) runs along the lower edge during the zoom in scenes 4 to 7: each zoom step shows the new pathogen beside the previous one at true relative scale where both can be seen in one frame (bacterium beside a red blood cell, at the start of scene 6; virus beside the bacterium; tobacco mosaic virus beside the coronavirus; viroid beside a virus; the prion is shown in its own half with a grey tag "one protein molecule: far smaller than a virus" and is not paired at scale, because a single protein would be a dot beside a virus), and uses a camera zoom where they cannot (tapeworm to tick to red blood cell). Plates are scaled proportionally, never stretched. Real organisms, cells and objects are painted plates; the tree, ruler, arrows, host circles, chips and glyph copies are coded. No people, hands, faces, patients or doctors. Hosts that are people are shown as abstract coded host circles only. Clutter rule (owner, 19 Oct): at most about three bright text items at once besides the small grey tree labels; tags fade when the next cue lands; branches not being spoken about dim to grey.
design.transitionPlan: The Fleming mould plate opens the hook with its clear ring and a penicillin tag; the definition writes on with pathogen and host labels; the SorterTree root writes and branches on the cells question; the tree shrinks to a thumbnail as the microorganism branch opens on the nucleus question with the bacterium, fungus and protozoan plates; a coded zoom-out sweep relabels the ruler in metres for the tapeworm and the external parasites; the zoom runs back in to a virus drawn at true scale beside the red blood cell and the TB rod; the viroid and prion halves open side by side; the full tree returns with plant slots beside each leaf; target chips light where a drug can act and dim where it cannot; four question chips write down the tree's left edge for the memory aid; each attempt clears the board and its feedback underlines the card as an AnsTable or two-column comparison fills; the decision rule chips and next chip close; scene crossfade with settle.
